title: Ang 1349–1350: Kabir in Prabhati
hookLine: first came the light; don't call the scriptures false
tomorrow: a man covered in holy marks, with a knife in his heart. who is he?

lines: EVERY HOLY BOOK IS MADE UP.
cards: Third period, and the argument is already going. Somebody in the back says every holy book is made up. Somebody else says only theirs isn't.
Phones out, voices up, the teacher tapping the board for quiet. Kabir's hymn on ang 1349 speaks into a room like that: people sure the other side's books were false. He doesn't pick a side.
He starts somewhere older than every book in the room.

teach.h: FROM ONE LIGHT, THE WHOLE WORLD.
teach.b: In paraphrase, the hymn opens: first God made the light, and all people are of God's making. From one light the whole world welled up. So who is good, and who is bad?

Notice the order. Before anyone's scripture, before anyone's label, there is light. Kabir calls God Allah here, and the light noor, words from the Muslim world, and he aims them at everyone listening.
One clay, shaped many ways by one Maker; there's no fault in the clay pots, and no fault in the Potter. Then, on the next page, in another hymn, the line that answers the classroom.
In paraphrase: don't call the Vedas and the other scriptures false.
False is the one who doesn't reflect. It's a careful line. Kabir doesn't say every book says the same thing.
He doesn't say books don't matter. He moves the word false off the page and onto the reader: the one who reads without looking inward. So the hymn's question comes back around.
Who's good, and who's bad? Kabir's answer is to look at where everyone came from.

how: Kabir's hymn 'from one light the whole world welled up' is sung in Prabhati, the dawn raga, and quoted in Sikh talks and kirtan on the oneness of people.

o: where Kabir says all people come from one light
where Guru Nanak opens the dawn raga Prabhati
where Farid's couplets begin in the Granth

games.q: Kabir's hymns on ang 1349–1350 — tap the pairs.

s: Kabir says the Vedas and the other scriptures are false
the opposite: don't call them false. false is the one who doesn't reflect.
the hymn calls God Allah, and the light noor
first God made the light; from one light the whole world welled up.
Kabir says every scripture teaches exactly the same thing
he says don't call them false. that's a different claim from 'all the same'.

games.q: one friend calls her grandmother's prayer book 'superstition.' another says only his own book is true. you get one sentence. what does Kabir's hymn give you?
o: start where everyone came from, one light; then ask who actually reflects on what they read.
tell them Kabir proved every religion is really one and the same religion.
stay out of it; Kabir says books don't matter, only the light inside does.
games.why: the hymn starts at the light, then moves 'false' off the book and onto the reader who won't reflect. it never says all the same, and never says books don't matter.

practice: Say the hymn's question out loud, slowly: from one light, who is good and who is bad? Then let the quiet hold it. If a face comes to mind, someone you've filed under bad, set it beside the word light and leave it there.

wordCard.voice: Ang 1349. Where Kabir, in the dawn raga, starts with the light, before anyone's book or label.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: ek noor, one light, from Kabir's hymn on ang 1349.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: first, the light, before anyone argued about whose book is true. See you at dawn.
